title_eng: XGBoost Regression of the Most Significant Photoplethysmogram Features for Assessing Vascular Aging
abstract:
3354 IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEAL TH INFORMA TICS, VOL. 26, NO. 7, JUL Y 2022
XGBoost Regression of the Most Signiﬁcant
Photoplethysmogram Features for
Assessing Vascular Aging
Hangsik Shin , Member, IEEE
Abstract— The purpose of this study was to conﬁrm
the potential of XGBoost as a vascular aging assessment
model based on the photoplethysmogram (PPG) features
suggested in previous studies, and to explore the key
PPG features for vascular aging assessment through
an explainable artiﬁcial intelligence method. The PPG
waveforms obtained from 752 volunteers aged 19–87 years
were analyzed and a total of 78 features were derived that
were proposed in previous studies. Age was estimated
through an XGBoost regression model, and estimation
error was calculated in terms of mean absolute error and
root-mean-squared error. To evaluate feature importance,
gain, coverage, weight, and SHAP value was calculated.
The vascular aging assessment model developed using
XGBoost has 8.1 years of mean-absolute error and 9.9
years of root-mean-squared error, a correlation coefﬁcient
of 0.63 with actual age, and a coefﬁcient of determination
of 0.39. Feature importance analysis using the SHAP value
conﬁrmed that features, such as systolic and diastolic peak
amplitude, risetime, skewness, and pulse area, play a key
role in vascular aging assessment. The XGBoost regres-
sion model showed an equal level of performance to the
existing PPG-based vascular aging assessment models.
Moreover, the result of feature importance analysis using
explainable artiﬁcial intelligence veriﬁed that the features
proposed in previous vascular aging assessment studies,
such as reﬂective index and risetime, were more important
in vascular aging assessment than other PPG features.
Index Terms — Explainable artiﬁcial intelligence,
photoplethysmogram, vascular aging, extreme gradient
boosting.

aging of the body does not show a noticeable change, it is
known as a major indicator that can inform the cardiovascular

risk directly related to life. V ascular ‘wear’, that is, vascular
aging, causes ‘hardening’ due to changes in the composition of
blood vessels, and is represented by vascular stiffness. In gen-
eral, elastin ﬁbers, a component of blood vessels, decrease with
age, or blood vessels become stiffer due to collagen cross-linking
caused by non-enzymatic glycation coupled with increasing
collagen concentration [1]. Pulse wave velocity (PWV) refers
to the speed of a pulse wave passing between two points in
the body [2], [3], which is known to be the most effective for
vascular stiffness assessment [4]–[8]. To measure PWV , distance
between two measuring sites should be known. However, it is
difﬁcult to accurately measure the distance between the two
points, because the points at which the pulse waves are recorded
are not in a straight line, or there is a difference depending on
the degree of obesity and curvature. Moreover, there is the in-
convenience of using the sensor, which is attached to two distant
points of the human body. Therefore, research to assess vascular
stiffness more conveniently is underway, and a method based
on photoplethysmogram (PPG) waveform analysis is attracting
attention [1], [9]–[17]. In a study that evaluated vascular stiffness
or vascular aging based on PPG, indicators for vascular aging
assessment were developed using the PPG waveform feature
points with the assumption that the PPG waveform is composed
of incident and reﬂected waves by pulse wave reﬂection at
the arterial branch, or using the differentiated PPG waveform
features. Representatively, Millasseau et al. used the two peaks
of the PPG waveform as a feature, and suggested the reﬂective
index (RI) as an index for reducing the reﬂected wave amplitude,
and the stiffness index (SI) as an index related to reﬂected wave
velocity, with a SI showing a correlation of 0.65 with PWV [10],
[12]. Meanwhile, Takazawa et al. developed multiple indices
combining the peak amplitudes of second-order differentiated
PPG, and showed that the combined index had a maximum cor-
relation coefﬁcient of 0.8 with age [17]. Recently, Park and Shin
proposed a method of estimating the age through a regression
equation using the characteristics of the separated waveform
after decomposing the PPG into incident wave and reﬂected
wave components, and showed that age can be estimated with
an error of about 10 years [13]. The vascular aging assessment
method based on PPG has been extensively investigated in recent
years; it is easier to create and evaluate signals than PWV and
can be easily adapted to a variety of portable wearable form
factors. However, unlike the existing vascular aging assessment
method based on PWV , which is based on the clear rationale

that ‘increases in vessel stiffness cause increases in intravascular
pressure and pulse wave velocity,’ the PPG method is based on
rather abstract grounds, such as incident and reﬂected waves,
differentiated PPG termed the acceleration plethysmogram, or
other morphologically presented waveform features. As a result,
in order to validate the hypothesis in previous studies and choose
effective features, it is required to study which characteristics
contributed the most to the evaluation of vascular aging through
an analysis of the numerous features offered to assess vascular
aging based on PPG. The goal of this study was to develop a
structure to assess vascular age using various features derived
from PPG waveform analysis, and to establish which features
have a close association with vascular aging by analyzing the
contributions of each feature. In this study, we developed a vas-
cular aging assessment model using Extreme Gradient Boosting
(XGBoost) [18], a regression model based on Ensemble Tree.
The waveform features of PPG, which are important for vascular
aging evaluation, was also explored by analyzing the contri-
bution of features used in model development using Shapley
Additive exPlanations (SHAP). It is a method that can explain
the classiﬁcation process of artiﬁcial intelligence [19].
II. M A TERIALS AND METHODS
A. Photoplethysmogram Waveform Feature
The waveform features were extracted from PPG by ana-
lyzing the PPG waveform. In preprocessing, recorded signals
were ﬁltered using a ﬁnite impulse response (FIR) bandpass
ﬁlter having a (0.5–10) Hz passband. Then, feature points were
extracted, such as the pulse onset, which represents the start
point of the pulsatile waveform, and the PPG was divided into
pulse segments based on the detected pulse onset. At this time, an
arrhythmic pulse segment with an abnormal range of pulse width
or pulse amplitude, or an abnormal pulse segment with a diastolic
peak amplitude greater than the systolic peak amplitude, was
excluded from the analysis. Because the number of samples for
each segment varied due to the pulse interval change, linear
interpolation was used to ensure that each segment had the same
number of samples as 1,000, and the amplitude was normalized
to be in the range of 0 to 1. Fig. 1 describes speciﬁc points of the
PPG waveform. The basic features were derived from the PPG
waveform and the features were combined by linear combination
of basic features as a photoplethysmographic feature for vascular
age evaluation. PPG spatiotemporal characteristics and incident
and reﬂected wave associated features generated from Gaussian
mixture model (GMM)-based waveform decomposition were
used in this study, which are the same as those proposed in our
previous study [13]. In the process of waveform decomposition
using GMM, the case where the correlation coefﬁcient between
the reconstructed pulse using the decomposed waveform and the
pulse of the original signal was less than 0.9 or the maximum
amplitude of the reﬂected wave was larger than the maximum
amplitude of the incident wave was excluded from the analysis.
Finally, a total of 78 candidate features that included 26 basic
features and 52 combined features were used as an input feature
of the XGBoost regression model. Table I– III lists the features.

B. Photoplethysmogram Waveform
The basic features were extracted from the PPG original
waveform. Fig. 1 shows that the PPG original waveform for
a pulsation usually has a rising–falling shape with two peaks;
whereby the ﬁrst peak is called a systolic peak, and the second
peak is called a diastolic peak. Usually, systolic peaks are clearly
distinguishable from all normal PPG waveforms, but diastolic
peaks may not be clearly observed depending on various phys-
iological conditions, such as the patient’s vascular stiffness.
As features of the original PPG waveform, this study used the
amplitude (Ampsys) and rising time (RTsys) of the systolic peak
at every beat, the diastolic peak amplitude ( Ampdia) and the
rising time ( RTdia), the area ( AreaPPG), and the pulse width
(PW PPG), kurtosis ( KurPPG), and skewness ( SkewPPG)o ft h e
PPG waveform (Table I).
C. Decomposed Photoplethysmogram
The main assumption of present vascular aging research is
the detailed component comprising the PPG waveform. Mil-
lasseau et al. and Y ousefet al. proposed the vascular aging eval-
uation indices based on the assumption that the PPG waveform
consists of the incident wave and reﬂected wave components
[10], [12], [16]. The main assumption of the existing vascular ag-
ing research is that the PPG waveform is composed of the sum of
sub-waveforms. Millasseau and Y ousef [10], [12], [16] proposed
the vascular aging assessment index from the assumption that
the PPG waveform consists of the incident wave and reﬂected
wave components. They assumed that the incident wave and the
reﬂected wave were represented by the systolic peak and dias-
tolic peak, respectively, of the PPG original waveform, and they
generated the vascular aging index from the characteristic fea-
